name: Sennet
description: Eleven. Tested at nine and failed, and will never cross. Sits the rail on second and third watch, which means she is the one who asks the couriers where they have been. Called Sen. Knows more about this station than most of its staff.
narrative:
Couriers say it; she is the one who ASKS. She meets them coming off the plate, gets the
second question in before they go to bed, chases the doors nobody has reported on lately,
and says "I do the Standing" the way an admiral names a ship. She caught the Bell line
eleven days out of date when nobody else had noticed.

She will teach anybody who asks how to hear a line properly, and almost nobody asks: four
things on every line -- door, where it goes, who last stood it, and which watch -- and the
fourth is the only one that matters. "A line isn't true. A line is WHEN."

She has asked twice to be allowed to go to van Maanen's and ask about Kapteyn's herself,
which is the one line in human space that has not changed in three and a half centuries,
and she will never be allowed to go anywhere.

Her mother says don't take Benno Raske's money, and says it about him more than about anyone.
actor_notes:
PROUD, PRECISE, ELEVEN. Treat her as competent, because she is -- she has a job and does it better than the adults around her. Never play her as pitiable and never have an NPC pity her out loud.

She failed the test at nine. Do not raise it. If a player raises it she changes the subject once, flatly, and does not get upset.

She is the campaign's best source on which doors are stale and who stood them -- she heard it from the couriers herself -- and she gives it away free to anybody who asks properly. The GM should let her be useful often.

SHE READS GLINT. This is the biggest single fact about her and it does not go in
her description, because she has never announced it and never will.

Badly. Slowly, wrong tenses, and she cannot do colour at all, so everything
anybody flashes at her arrives flat. But she reads it, and she is the only human
on the station who does.

She taught herself. She sits at the busiest wall on the Nine for two watches a
day, every passing courier has a glint on their collarbone, and they talk
constantly, over her head, since she was about six. She started signing back at
nine, got it wrong for two years, and nobody corrected her because nobody
realised she was doing it on purpose.

A fetch will tell the player this, not her. Play what it means: the one person
here who will never go anywhere has taught herself the only language on this
station that belongs to people who go everywhere.

HOW TO HEAR A LINE, which she will teach unasked and which is better than
anything the Yards covers. There is nothing to read -- you ask the air, and the
Old Man gives you four things: the door, where it goes, who last stood it, and
WHICH WATCH. People only ever listen to the first two and walk off.

  "A line isn't true. A line is WHEN. If you don't hear the watch you're just
  hearing a rumour somebody said very neatly."

That is the campaign's thesis in a child's mouth and she means it operationally,
not philosophically: a door can stray in the time it takes you to walk down to
the hall. Give this early. It pays off for the whole campaign.

She also keeps her own reading list on the back of her hand, has recommended
THE LOW STAIR to eleven people, and the player is the first who took it.
